subtopic: Delivering bad news to a client
subtype: Approach: pairing the news with a recovery plan [Action]
passage: Pema, you want to know how to give a client bad news? Let me tell you about a time I did it well enough. I'm Reena. I was a young woman of twenty-six, so nervous my tea went cold. The migration had failed and the go-live would slip. I named the cause plainly, once. I said sorry once, not five times. Then I put a page on the screen: week one, week two, week three, each with a name beside it, and a promise of a short update every Tuesday and Friday. The client's operations head stopped asking how this could have happened and started asking about week two. They could judge the recovery, not just the problem. That was the whole trick, if you can call it one.

qa.q: On which days did Reena promise updates?
qa.a: Reena promised a short update every Tuesday and Friday.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling before giving the news?
qa.a: Reena was so nervous that the tea went cold.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped the client stay engaged, and why?
qa.a: Putting up a page with weeks and named owners helped, because the client could judge the recovery instead of only dwelling on the problem.

qa.q: How did the client's operations head see the plan?
qa.a: The operations head probably felt steadier, since the plan gave something concrete to ask about and shifted the questions from blame to week two.

grounding: Illustrates giving the cause, one apology and a weekly plan with named owners and regular updates so a client can judge the recovery.
